shortlist.raw_text: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.

shortlist.raw_text: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.

Title: Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia

Text:
When investors get nervous about AI spending, it helps to have the chipmaker that sells the chips offer to cosign the loan.

Article text (excerpt):
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday . Bloomberg later corroborated the report. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing . In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.
The proposed arrangement would help Nscale secure financing for the electricity and construction costs of its West Virginia campus. Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information .
Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.
The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.
Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. The companies are also discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion for another building.
Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground. The company had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August , a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy. Its West Virginia campus has run into trouble of its own. Runoff from the construction site has flooded nearby homes more than once . In September, after months of negotiations , the project won state certification.
This month, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.
Nvidia has been a major financial backer of the sector, extending roughly $170 billion in investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers, according to The Information. That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.
Neoclouds, which rent out AI computing power without a cash-rich core business behind them, have come under pressure from investors. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN had each fallen more than 30% in October as of last week, CNBC reported .
The proposed guarantee would deepen Nvidia’s financial ties to Nscale while helping secure a major customer for its chips. Anthropic, one of the largest buyers of AI computing power, has spread its infrastructure spending across multiple chipmakers. One investor told The Information that Anthropic’s involvement likely explains Nvidia’s interest in keeping Nscale’s project on track.
The discussions also come as Anthropic faces questions about how it will finance its own rapid expansion. The company filed to go public this week, but Blackstone has warned investors that Anthropic may receive a below-investment-grade credit rating after its IPO. A junk rating would raise Anthropic’s borrowing costs and could push it to keep relying on stronger partners to back its debt.

text:
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt for a data center builder.

Anthropic signed a $44.6 billion contract for the site, but the builder cannot cover construction costs alone.

Here is how the deal works.

The company constructing the facility is Nscale, an AI cloud provider seeking an IPO at up to a $35 billion valuation.

It plans to deploy nearly 500,000 advanced chips, but had only 25,000 running in August.

To keep the West Virginia project moving, Nvidia is considering a residual value guarantee.

If Nscale defaults on construction payments, Nvidia would step in, temporarily take over the building, and find a new tenant.

Nvidia previously backed chip purchases and leases, but not construction costs.

The arrangement secures infrastructure for a major buyer:
• Anthropic signed a $44.6 billion contract for the first 460-megawatt building
• The facility is designed to run Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips
• The companies are discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion

Nvidia has already extended roughly $170 billion in investments and credit support across the sector.

Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN each fell more than 30% in October as investors grew cautious about spending.

My read: when chip sellers start guaranteeing construction loans, the barrier to AI expansion is no longer engineering. It is balance sheets.

Would you trust a tech boom where the supplier acts as the bank?

Source: TechCrunch

Option 1 (Bare number first):
$44.6 billion for a single data center building.
Anthropic signed the contract, but the builder now needs the chipmaker to co-sign its construction loans.
• When to prefer: Use this when the raw monetary value is large enough to create immediate curiosity before any context is given.

Option 2 (Corrective):
Nvidia is no longer just selling chips to data centers.
It is now considering co-signing billions in debt to build the brick-and-mortar facilities that house them.
• When to prefer: Use this when writing for corporate or finance professionals who will instantly grasp the shift in business strategy.

Option 3 (Your X):
Your next AI model might run on infrastructure backed by mortgage-style guarantees.
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee debt for a supplier that has struggled to get its own sites built.
• When to prefer: Use this when targeting end-users or managers focused on the long-term operational risk of their AI tools.

Pick: Option 2, because it highlights the strategic shift in how AI infrastructure is being funded before the reader clicks "see more".
